dc_comics.name: DC Comics
dc_comics.desc:
The American comic book publisher that grew out of Malcolm Wheeler-Nicholson's National Allied Publications, founded in 1934. The company took its familiar initials from its flagship title, Detective Comics, and used DC as a cover logo for decades before formally adopting the name DC Comics in 1977.

Through a chain of mergers it absorbed its sister firm All-American Publications in 1946 and was reorganised as National Comics Publications, then National Periodical Publications. Its characters — Superman, Batman and Wonder Woman above all — became the founding archetypes of the superhero genre, and its corporate history since 1967 has been that of a subsidiary inside a succession of ever larger media conglomerates.

national_allied_publications.name: National Allied Publications
national_allied_publications.desc:
The company founded in 1934 by Malcolm Wheeler-Nicholson, and the direct corporate ancestor of DC Comics. Its first release, New Fun #1 in early 1935, was among the first American comic books to carry entirely original material rather than reprinted newspaper strips.

Chronically undercapitalised, National Allied depended on the printing and distribution services of Harry Donenfeld and the bookkeeping of Jack Liebowitz. Wheeler-Nicholson was forced out in 1938 and the firm was folded into the business that became DC.

detective_comics_inc.name: Detective Comics, Inc.
detective_comics_inc.desc:
The partnership formed in 1937 between Malcolm Wheeler-Nicholson and the Donenfeld-Liebowitz business to launch a third title when National Allied could not fund it alone. The company published Detective Comics #1 in March 1938.

Within a year Wheeler-Nicholson had been bought out and Donenfeld and Liebowitz controlled both companies outright. The corporate name survived as the source of the two letters — DC — under which the publisher would eventually be known worldwide.

all_american_publications.name: All-American Publications
all_american_publications.desc:
A sister company set up in 1939 by Max Gaines with financial backing from Jack Liebowitz, operating from separate offices with Sheldon Mayer as editor. Legally distinct but marketed jointly, All-American shared the DC cover logo and the two lines were widely read as one publisher.

All-American produced a remarkable share of the Golden Age canon: Flash Comics, All-American Comics, All Star Comics, Green Lantern and Wonder Woman. Gaines sold his interest in 1946 and the company was absorbed into National Comics Publications, unifying the two halves of what became DC.

fawcett_comics.name: Fawcett Comics
fawcett_comics.desc:
The comics division of Fawcett Publications, whose Captain Marvel outsold Superman during the 1940s and became the best-selling superhero of the decade. Whiz Comics, Captain Marvel Adventures and the wider Marvel Family made Fawcett DC's most serious commercial rival.

National sued Fawcett for infringing Superman, and after more than a decade of litigation Fawcett settled and stopped publishing superhero comics in 1953. DC licensed the characters in 1972 and bought them outright in 1991 — an acquisition of the very property it had once sued out of existence.

charlton_comics.name: Charlton Comics
charlton_comics.desc:
A Connecticut publisher that printed its own comics on presses originally bought for song lyric magazines, paying low rates but allowing unusual creative freedom. Its 1960s action-hero line included Steve Ditko's Blue Beetle and the Question, along with Captain Atom, Nightshade, Peacemaker and Thunderbolt.

Charlton left comics publishing in the mid-1980s and DC bought its superhero characters in 1983. The purchase had an outsized consequence: Alan Moore's proposal to use the newly acquired heroes was redirected into original analogues, producing Watchmen.

ec_comics.name: EC Comics
ec_comics.desc:
The publisher Max Gaines founded after selling his stake in All-American, originally issuing educational and Bible comics. Under his son William Gaines it became EC — home of Tales from the Crypt, Weird Science and Mad — and the most artistically admired line of the early 1950s.

EC's horror and crime titles were the central target of the 1954 anti-comics campaign, and the Comics Code destroyed its business model. The company survived only through Mad, which converted to magazine format to escape the Code; Mad was later bought by DC's parent and published alongside DC for decades.

warner_communications.name: Warner Communications
warner_communications.desc:
The conglomerate that has owned DC since 1967, when Kinney National Company acquired National Periodical Publications. Kinney bought Warner Bros.-Seven Arts in 1969 and renamed itself Warner Communications in 1972, placing the comics publisher inside a company that also owned a film studio, a record business and, later, a cable network.

Corporate ownership passed through Time Warner, AT&T's WarnerMedia and, from 2022, Warner Bros. Discovery. The arrangement made DC's characters film and television assets as much as publishing ones, and increasingly shaped editorial strategy around screen exploitation.

vertigo.name: Vertigo
vertigo.desc:
The adult-oriented imprint launched in 1993 under executive editor Karen Berger, gathering the mature titles she had already been editing — Sandman, Hellblazer, Swamp Thing, Doom Patrol — under one banner published without the Comics Code seal.

Vertigo institutionalised the British invasion of American comics and a creator-driven model with better rights terms than DC's superhero line, producing Preacher, Y: The Last Man, Fables, Transmetropolitan and 100 Bullets. Berger left in 2013; DC announced the imprint's closure in 2019 and it stopped publishing in January 2020, with its function passing to DC Black Label and Young Animal. The name was revived in 2024.

wildstorm.name: WildStorm
wildstorm.desc:
Jim Lee's studio, founded in 1992 as one of the constituent parts of Image Comics, publishing WildC.A.T.s, Gen 13 and later the Warren Ellis-driven titles The Authority and Planetary that reshaped superhero storytelling in the late 1990s.

Lee sold WildStorm to DC in a deal agreed in 1998 and effective from January 1999. The deal brought DC a sub-imprint, the Homage and America's Best Comics lines, and — most consequentially — Lee himself, who moved from studio owner to DC's best-known artist and eventually to its senior creative leadership.

milestone_media.name: Milestone Media
milestone_media.desc:
A Black-owned comics company founded in 1993 by Dwayne McDuffie, Denys Cowan, Michael Davis and Derek T. Dingle, created to put characters of colour at the centre of a superhero universe rather than at its margins.

Milestone retained ownership of its characters while DC handled publishing and distribution, an unusual arrangement for the period. Its line included Icon, Hardware, Blood Syndicate and Static, whose animated adaptation Static Shock reached a far larger audience than the comics. The imprint wound down in the later 1990s and was revived with DC in 2021.

dc_studios.name: DC Studios
dc_studios.desc:
The Warner Bros. Discovery division established in 2022 with James Gunn and Peter Safran as co-chairs, given authority over DC film, television and animation in order to end the fragmented approach of the previous decade.

Its remit was to build a single planned continuity across media, beginning with the 2025 film Superman. The creation of DC Studios marked the point at which the screen operation, rather than the publishing arm, became the principal steward of the characters.

golden_age.name: The Golden Age
golden_age.desc:
The period from roughly 1938 to the mid-1950s in which the superhero was invented and the American comic book became a mass medium, selling in the millions to children and to servicemen during the Second World War.

For DC the era begins with Action Comics #1 and runs through Batman, Wonder Woman, the Justice Society and a crowded field of costumed imitators. The boom collapsed after the war as readers turned to crime, romance, western and horror titles, and by the early 1950s only Superman, Batman and Wonder Woman were still published continuously.

silver_age.name: The Silver Age
silver_age.desc:
The revival of the superhero from the mid-1950s, conventionally dated at DC to Showcase #4 in 1956, in which editor Julius Schwartz reintroduced the Flash as a new character with a science-fiction origin rather than reviving the old one.

The formula — bright, rationalised, aimed squarely at children under the Comics Code — produced a new Green Lantern, the Justice League, and eventually the multiverse, which allowed the Golden Age heroes to return as inhabitants of a parallel Earth. DC's success with the Justice League is widely credited with prompting the rival line that became Marvel.

bronze_age.name: The Bronze Age
bronze_age.desc:
The period from about 1970 to the mid-1980s in which superhero comics took on social subject matter, darker art and more continuity-heavy storytelling, while the newsstand audience shrank and the direct market of specialist shops began to replace it.

At DC the era is marked by Denny O'Neil and Neal Adams returning Batman to the night, their Green Lantern/Green Arrow road stories about racism, poverty and addiction, Jack Kirby's Fourth World, and the arrival of a generation of writers and artists who would demand royalties and creator credit.

fredric_wertham.name: Fredric Wertham
fredric_wertham.desc:
A German-American psychiatrist who ran clinics serving poor and largely Black patients in Harlem and who campaigned through the late 1940s and early 1950s against comic books as a cause of juvenile delinquency.

His testimony and writing gave scientific respectability to a broad public campaign against the medium. Later examination of his surviving research files found that he had overstated and reshaped case material to fit his conclusions, though his influence on the industry at the time was decisive and lasting.

seduction_of_the_innocent.name: Seduction of the Innocent
seduction_of_the_innocent.desc:
Fredric Wertham's 1954 book arguing that comic books taught children violence, sadism and sexual deviance, illustrated with panels reproduced out of context. It included readings of Batman and Robin as a coded homosexual household and of Wonder Woman as a figure of bondage and man-hating.

A bestseller that fed directly into United States Senate subcommittee hearings on juvenile delinquency the same year, the book pushed publishers into pre-emptive self-regulation and shaped what American comics could depict for the next two decades.

comics_code_authority.name: Comics Code Authority
comics_code_authority.desc:
The self-censorship body created in 1954 by the Comics Magazine Association of America in response to the anti-comics campaign and the threat of legislation. Its code banned horror and crime titles outright, forbade sympathetic criminals, and required that authority always be respected and evil always punished.

Distributors refused unsealed comics, so compliance was effectively compulsory. DC, whose wholesome house style was already close to the Code's requirements, was among the least damaged publishers and became one of the system's staunchest supporters. DC finally abandoned the seal in 2011.

malcolm_wheeler_nicholson.name: Malcolm Wheeler-Nicholson
malcolm_wheeler_nicholson.desc:
A former United States cavalry officer and pulp adventure writer who founded National Allied Publications in 1934, becoming the first publisher to build a comic book line on original material rather than newspaper strip reprints.

His instinct for the form was better than his finances. Unable to pay printers or contributors, he took Harry Donenfeld as a partner on Detective Comics and was squeezed out of his own company in 1938, months before Superman made it rich. He received nothing from the character's success and died in relative obscurity in 1965.

harry_donenfeld.name: Harry Donenfeld
harry_donenfeld.desc:
A printer and pulp magazine publisher whose Independent News distribution arm gave him leverage over the struggling comic book firms he serviced. He took control of Detective Comics, Inc. and then of National Allied after Wheeler-Nicholson's bankruptcy.

Donenfeld was the public face of the company through the Superman boom while Jack Liebowitz ran the business. He presided over the purchase of Superman for a flat fee and the litigation that followed, and remained president until ill health ended his involvement in the early 1960s.

jack_liebowitz.name: Jack Liebowitz
jack_liebowitz.desc:
An accountant who became Donenfeld's partner and the operational mind of the company for three decades, financing All-American Publications, consolidating the two lines in 1946, and steering National Periodical Publications through the Code years.

He negotiated the 1967 sale to Kinney National Company and joined its board, converting a comic book firm into a media asset. Cautious, litigious and commercially shrewd, he did more than anyone to make DC an institution — and was the executive most directly responsible for keeping Siegel and Shuster from any share of Superman.

max_gaines.name: Max Gaines
max_gaines.desc:
A salesman usually credited with proving that reprinted newspaper strips could be sold as a standalone magazine, an insight that helped create the American comic book. He worked as a middleman and packager before founding All-American Publications in 1939 with Liebowitz's money.

Gaines is also credited with passing the Superman submission along to National after seeing it. He sold his All-American interest in 1946 and started what became EC Comics, dying in a boating accident in 1947 and leaving the company to his son William.

jenette_kahn.name: Jenette Kahn
jenette_kahn.desc:
A magazine publisher hired in 1976, at twenty-eight, to run a DC that was losing badly to Marvel. She served as publisher, then president, and finally president and editor-in-chief until 2002 — the longest and most transformative executive tenure in the company's history.

Kahn introduced royalties and creator incentives, restored Siegel and Shuster's credit and pensions, recruited British writers, backed the direct market, and gave editorial room to the books that became The Dark Knight Returns, Watchmen and Vertigo. She turned DC from an imitator of Marvel into the industry's prestige publisher.

paul_levitz.name: Paul Levitz
paul_levitz.desc:
A fanzine editor who joined DC in 1973 and spent more than three decades there as writer, editor and executive, serving as president and publisher from 2002 to 2009 — one of the few people to hold both a long creative and a long corporate career at the company.

As a writer he is best known for a lengthy Legion of Super-Heroes run including The Great Darkness Saga. As an executive he helped design the royalty and creator-rights reforms of the Kahn era and stabilised DC's business through the direct market's boom and its 1990s collapse.

whitney_ellsworth.name: Whitney Ellsworth
whitney_ellsworth.desc:
DC's editorial director from 1940, the executive who set the house standards that governed the company through the Golden Age. He drafted an internal code restricting violence, gore and sexual suggestion well before the industry adopted one, which left DC comparatively unscathed when the Comics Code arrived.

Ellsworth moved to Hollywood to supervise DC's screen properties, producing the Superman film serials' successors and the Adventures of Superman television series. He is the figure who first made the company think of its characters as licensable assets rather than magazine content.

sheldon_mayer.name: Sheldon Mayer
sheldon_mayer.desc:
A cartoonist who became Max Gaines's editor at All-American Publications while still in his twenties, overseeing Flash Comics, All-American Comics, All Star Comics and the arrival of Wonder Woman.

By his own later account, Mayer retrieved the rejected Superman strip from a discard pile and pressed Gaines to push it forward. He left editing to return to drawing, producing the long-running children's humour strip Sugar and Spike, and remains one of the few Golden Age figures respected equally as an editor and as a cartoonist.

mort_weisinger.name: Mort Weisinger
mort_weisinger.desc:
A science fiction fan and agent who joined the company in 1941 and edited the Superman line for most of three decades. He co-created Aquaman and Green Arrow before turning to the work that defined him: the systematic construction of a Superman mythology.

Under Weisinger came Supergirl, Krypto, the Bottle City of Kandor, the Fortress of Solitude, Bizarro, red and gold kryptonite and the Legion of Super-Heroes — an elaborate internally consistent world built from reader-suggestion letters. He was also notorious among his writers as a harsh and belittling editor.

julius_schwartz.name: Julius Schwartz
julius_schwartz.desc:
A science fiction literary agent turned comics editor whose 1956 decision to revive the Flash as an entirely new character with a new secret identity is the conventional starting point of the Silver Age.

Schwartz repeated the method with Green Lantern, Hawkman and the Atom, commissioned the Justice League, and authorised the parallel-Earth story that created DC's multiverse. In 1964 he took over a flagging Batman and instituted the New Look. He later edited the Superman titles for years, closing that era with Alan Moore's Whatever Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?

dick_giordano.name: Dick Giordano
dick_giordano.desc:
An inker and editor who came to DC in 1968 from Charlton, bringing with him several younger creators including Denny O'Neil and Steve Skeates. He inked much of Neal Adams's DC work and formed a studio partnership with him in the 1970s.

Returning as an executive, Giordano was DC's editorial leader from 1983 to 1993, the period that produced Crisis on Infinite Earths, the Byrne Superman relaunch, The Dark Knight Returns, Watchmen, Batman: Year One and the mature-readers line that became Vertigo. Few editors have presided over a comparable run.

karen_berger.name: Karen Berger
karen_berger.desc:
The editor who recruited Alan Moore to Swamp Thing and then, acting as DC's talent scout in Britain, brought over Neil Gaiman, Grant Morrison, Jamie Delano, Peter Milligan and others.

In 1993 she consolidated the mature-readers titles she had been editing into Vertigo and ran the imprint as executive editor for twenty years, giving creators unusual freedom and better rights terms. Sandman, Preacher, Y: The Last Man and Fables were all published on her watch; the imprint's literary reputation is largely her editorial signature.

jerry_siegel.name: Jerry Siegel
jerry_siegel.desc:
The Cleveland science fiction fan who conceived Superman with his schoolfriend Joe Shuster around 1933 and spent five years failing to sell him as a newspaper strip before the pair placed the material with National in 1938.

Siegel and Shuster signed away the character for 130 dollars and page rates, and litigated repeatedly for the rest of their lives to reclaim it. They were removed from the Superman titles in the late 1940s after suing, and Siegel spent years out of comics. A public campaign in 1975 secured pensions and the restoration of their creator credit on every Superman story.

bill_finger.name: Bill Finger
bill_finger.desc:
The writer who turned Bob Kane's initial sketch of a red-suited bird-themed hero into Batman: the cowl, the cape, the grey and black costume, the name Bruce Wayne, Gotham City, the detective emphasis and much of the supporting cast and rogues' gallery.

Kane's contract gave him sole credit, and Finger worked without a byline on Batman for the rest of his life, dying in poverty in 1974. After decades of campaigning, largely by his family and by fellow professionals, DC agreed in 2015 to credit Batman as created by Bob Kane with Bill Finger.

william_moulton_marston.name: William Moulton Marston
william_moulton_marston.desc:
A Harvard-trained psychologist, a developer of systolic blood pressure deception testing that fed into the polygraph, and a popular writer on psychology who was hired by Max Gaines as a consultant after publicly defending comics.

Marston proposed a female hero who would conquer through love rather than force, and wrote Wonder Woman under the pen name Charles Moulton from 1941 until his death in 1947, drawn throughout by H. G. Peter. The strip's feminism, its unconventional domestic origins in Marston's own household, and its recurring bondage imagery have been debated ever since.

gardner_fox.name: Gardner Fox
gardner_fox.desc:
One of the most prolific writers in comics, credited with thousands of stories across four decades and with much of DC's structural imagination. He created the Flash, Hawkman, Doctor Fate, the Sandman and the Justice Society of America — comics' first superhero team — in the Golden Age.

Returning under Julius Schwartz, he wrote the Justice League of America from its 1960 debut and invented DC's multiverse in Flash of Two Worlds, which let the Golden Age heroes exist on a parallel Earth. He also co-created Barbara Gordon's Batgirl. He left DC in 1968 after pressing for health benefits.

john_broome.name: John Broome
john_broome.desc:
A quiet and widely travelled writer who was Julius Schwartz's principal scripter through the early Silver Age, giving the revived heroes their tone of brisk, good-humoured pseudo-science.

With Gil Kane he co-created Hal Jordan's Green Lantern and the Green Lantern Corps, Sinestro and the Guardians of the Universe; with Carmine Infantino he built most of the Flash's rogues gallery, including Captain Cold, Gorilla Grodd and the Reverse-Flash, and wrote Flash of Two Worlds from Fox's premise of parallel Earths. He left comics in the 1970s to teach abroad.

denny_oneil.name: Denny O'Neil
denny_oneil.desc:
A former journalist who became the defining writer of DC's Bronze Age. With Neal Adams he stripped the camp from Batman and returned him to a grim night-time detective, and sent Green Lantern and Green Arrow across America in stories about racism, poverty, pollution and heroin addiction.

He co-created Ra's al Ghul, Talia, John Stewart and the modern Two-Face characterisation, and wrote the Question and Iron Man. As Batman group editor from 1986 to 2000 he oversaw Year One, A Death in the Family, Knightfall and No Man's Land.

len_wein.name: Len Wein
len_wein.desc:
A writer and editor who moved fluently between DC and Marvel, co-creating Swamp Thing with Bernie Wrightson at DC and Wolverine and the revived X-Men at Marvel — an unusual double claim on two companies' most valuable properties.

At DC he wrote Justice League of America, co-created Amanda Waller for the Suicide Squad, and edited Watchmen, where his early editorial pressure shaped the series' structure. He also scripted the framing text pieces and, later in life, returned to write Swamp Thing again.

marv_wolfman.name: Marv Wolfman
marv_wolfman.desc:
The writer who gave DC its biggest commercial success of the early 1980s. With George Pérez he relaunched the Teen Titans as The New Teen Titans in 1980, creating Raven, Cyborg and Starfire and building a soap-operatic ensemble that finally rivalled Marvel's X-Men in sales.

Wolfman then conceived and wrote Crisis on Infinite Earths, the twelve-issue series that demolished the multiverse he had inherited and rebuilt DC's continuity from scratch. He also created Blade at Marvel and later wrote extensively for animation.

alan_moore.name: Alan Moore
alan_moore.desc:
The British writer whose arrival at DC in 1983 changed what mainstream superhero comics were assumed to be capable of. His Swamp Thing dismantled the character's premise in a single issue and rebuilt him as an elemental, and introduced John Constantine.

With Dave Gibbons he wrote Watchmen, the most acclaimed work the medium has produced. He also wrote The Killing Joke, For the Man Who Has Everything and Whatever Happened to the Man of Tomorrow? Disputes over the Watchmen rights reversion and over merchandising ended his relationship with DC, and he has since refused credit or payment for adaptations.

frank_miller.name: Frank Miller
frank_miller.desc:
A writer-artist who came to DC after redefining Daredevil at Marvel. Batman: The Dark Knight Returns, published in 1986, imagined an ageing Batman returning to a decayed Gotham and recast the character as a figure of grim, contested authority.

With David Mazzucchelli he then wrote Batman: Year One, which became the accepted account of the character's first year. Together with Watchmen, The Dark Knight Returns is credited with — and blamed for — the darker, more adult register that dominated superhero comics for the following decade.

grant_morrison.name: Grant Morrison
grant_morrison.desc:
A Scottish writer recruited to DC in the late 1980s, whose Animal Man and Doom Patrol turned superhero comics into vehicles for metafiction and surrealism, and whose The Invisibles anchored Vertigo's most experimental period.

Morrison also wrote at DC's commercial centre: JLA restored the Justice League as a pantheon of gods, All-Star Superman distilled the character to his essentials, and Batman R.I.P., Final Crisis and the introduction of Damian Wayne reshaped both flagship franchises. Their work characteristically treats continuity as a resource rather than an obstacle.

neil_gaiman.name: Neil Gaiman
neil_gaiman.desc:
A British journalist and writer brought to DC by Karen Berger, who took a minor Golden Age title and produced The Sandman: seventy-five issues, ending in 1996, about Dream of the Endless and the limits of change.

Sandman drew an audience that had not previously read comics, was unusually widely read by women, and became the commercial foundation and the argument for Vertigo. Gaiman also wrote Black Orchid, Signal to Noise and the Batman story Whatever Happened to the Caped Crusader?, before moving primarily to prose fiction.

geoff_johns.name: Geoff Johns
geoff_johns.desc:
The writer most responsible for DC's direction through the 2000s and 2010s, known for taking discarded or damaged characters and restoring them by treating their continuity as an asset. He returned Hal Jordan to the Green Lantern books and built the emotional spectrum and Blackest Night around him.

He wrote Infinite Crisis, Flashpoint — which triggered the New 52 relaunch — and DC Universe: Rebirth #1, which reversed much of it. Johns also served as DC's chief creative officer, extending his influence over the company's film and television output.

john_ostrander.name: John Ostrander
john_ostrander.desc:
A playwright turned comics writer whose 1987 Suicide Squad took a forgotten 1950s title and turned it into a black-ops political thriller in which convicted supervillains ran deniable missions for the American government and were killed off without warning.

Ostrander built the series around Amanda Waller, an unglamorous, uncompromising bureaucrat who remains one of DC's most durable original characters. He also wrote The Spectre, Firestorm and Grimjack, and his Squad is the direct source of the character's later film and television versions.

scott_snyder.name: Scott Snyder
scott_snyder.desc:
A short story writer who became DC's flagship Batman writer at the New 52 relaunch in 2011, running with artist Greg Capullo for five years — one of the longest continuous creative teams on the title.

His Court of Owls introduced a secret society claiming to have run Gotham for centuries, arguing that Batman had never truly known his own city, and Death of the Family returned the Joker to outright horror. Snyder later wrote the Dark Nights: Metal event and Justice League, and has since concentrated on creator-owned work.

dwayne_mcduffie.name: Dwayne McDuffie
dwayne_mcduffie.desc:
A writer and editor who co-founded Milestone Media in 1993 to create a superhero universe in which characters of colour were central rather than tokenised, and who wrote much of its line including Icon and Hardware.

McDuffie went on to become one of the most influential writers in superhero animation, story editing and writing Static Shock and Justice League Unlimited, where he made John Stewart, Hawkgirl and Amanda Waller familiar to a mass audience. He died in 2011; Milestone's characters were later folded into DC's main continuity.

joe_shuster.name: Joe Shuster
joe_shuster.desc:
The artist half of the Superman partnership, who drew the character from the first Cleveland sketches through Action Comics #1 and the early years of the strip, establishing the cape, the chest emblem, the leap and the visual grammar of the superhero.

His eyesight failed steadily and he was largely out of comics by the 1950s, working in obscurity and poor health. With Siegel he pursued decades of unsuccessful litigation over Superman before the 1975 campaign secured both men a pension and permanent creator credit from Warner.

bob_kane.name: Bob Kane
bob_kane.desc:
The cartoonist credited as Batman's creator, who brought an initial concept to editor Vin Sullivan in 1939 and then developed it with Bill Finger, whose contributions were decisive and uncredited.

Kane negotiated an unusually strong contract giving him a sole byline and a share of the character, and for decades signed work substantially produced by ghost artists including Jerry Robinson, Sheldon Moldoff and Dick Sprang. He remained a public figure associated with Batman until his death in 1998. DC added Finger's name to the credit line in 2015.

jerry_robinson.name: Jerry Robinson
jerry_robinson.desc:
Hired at seventeen to letter and ink for Bob Kane, Robinson became a central figure of the early Batman studio and is credited by most accounts with the playing-card idea that produced the Joker, and with naming Dick Grayson.

He later worked as an illustrator, cartoonist and comics historian, and served as president of the National Cartoonists Society. In 1975 he led the public campaign, with Neal Adams, that forced Warner to grant Siegel and Shuster pensions and credit — an early and rare victory for creators' rights in the industry.

curt_swan.name: Curt Swan
curt_swan.desc:
The artist who drew Superman for roughly thirty years from the mid-1950s and whose clean, warm, unexaggerated figure work became the definitive look of the character for two generations of readers.

Swan illustrated the entire Weisinger mythos and stayed through the Schwartz era, closing it by drawing Alan Moore's Whatever Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?, the story that formally ended the pre-Crisis Superman in 1986. His style is the visual baseline against which every later Superman artist has been measured.

carmine_infantino.name: Carmine Infantino
carmine_infantino.desc:
The artist whose sleek, streamlined design work opened the Silver Age: he drew Showcase #4, redesigned the Flash's costume, and gave DC's revived heroes their modern look. He also drew the New Look Batman and co-created Barbara Gordon's Batgirl and Deadman.

Infantino moved into management as editorial director in 1967 and then publisher until 1976 — the rare artist to run a major comics company. He recruited Jack Kirby to DC, but the period was commercially difficult and he returned to drawing afterwards.

gil_kane.name: Gil Kane
gil_kane.desc:
A draughtsman admired for dynamic anatomy and dramatic low-angle figures, who with John Broome designed and drew the Silver Age Green Lantern — the crew-cut test pilot Hal Jordan and the sleek green and black costume that replaced Alan Scott's Golden Age design.

Kane also drew the Atom's revival, worked extensively at Marvel, and produced His Name Is... Savage and Blackmark, early attempts at the graphic novel format that anticipated the market by a decade.

neal_adams.name: Neal Adams
neal_adams.desc:
The artist whose photographic realism and cinematic staging broke DC's flat house style at the end of the 1960s. With Denny O'Neil he returned Batman to a gaunt night-time figure and drew the Green Lantern/Green Arrow stories that brought social subject matter into mainstream superhero comics.

Adams was equally consequential as an activist: he campaigned for original art to be returned to artists, for page-rate and royalty reform, and led the 1975 effort with Jerry Robinson that won Siegel and Shuster their pensions and credit.

jack_kirby.name: Jack Kirby
jack_kirby.desc:
The artist who had co-created most of the Marvel universe and who left it for DC in 1970 in a dispute over credit and ownership, recruited by Carmine Infantino with the promise of writing, drawing and editing his own titles.

The result was the Fourth World — New Gods, Mister Miracle, The Forever People and a retooled Superman's Pal Jimmy Olsen — an interlocking modern mythology introducing Darkseid, Apokolips and New Genesis. Commercially disappointing and cancelled early, it became one of the most influential bodies of work in the medium.

bernie_wrightson.name: Bernie Wrightson
bernie_wrightson.desc:
A horror artist of exceptional line control who co-created Swamp Thing with Len Wein in 1971, first in a standalone House of Secrets story and then in the ongoing series, establishing the moody Louisiana-gothic register the character has kept ever since.

Wrightson left the title after ten issues and spent much of the following decade on a set of detailed pen-and-ink illustrations for Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, widely regarded as his masterwork. His influence runs through nearly all later horror comics art.

george_perez.name: George Pérez
george_perez.desc:
An artist celebrated for dense, meticulous crowd scenes and for drawing large casts without losing individual character. With Marv Wolfman he co-created The New Teen Titans in 1980 and then drew Crisis on Infinite Earths, a series that required rendering essentially every character DC owned.

After Crisis he wrote and drew the relaunched Wonder Woman, rebuilding her around Greek myth and taking her seriously as a mythological figure for the first time in decades. He later drew The Infinity Gauntlet at Marvel and returned for Infinite Crisis.

dave_gibbons.name: Dave Gibbons
dave_gibbons.desc:
The British artist who drew Watchmen, whose disciplined nine-panel grid, controlled colour and buried visual repetitions are inseparable from the work's meaning — the formal argument that the series makes as much as its script.

Gibbons came to DC from 2000 AD alongside the other British recruits of the mid-1980s and also drew Green Lantern, Superman and, with Frank Miller, Martha Washington. He was the only principal Watchmen creator to remain on speaking terms with DC after the dispute over the property.

john_byrne.name: John Byrne
john_byrne.desc:
A writer-artist who arrived from Marvel, where his Uncanny X-Men and Fantastic Four runs had made him one of the industry's biggest names, to restart Superman after Crisis on Infinite Earths.

His 1986 miniseries The Man of Steel rebuilt the character from the ground up: Krypton cold and sterile, the Kents alive into Clark's adulthood, no super-career as Superboy, Lex Luthor recast as a corrupt billionaire, and Clark rather than Superman as the real identity. The template governed the character for twenty-five years.

jim_lee.name: Jim Lee
jim_lee.desc:
The best-selling artist of the early 1990s, who left Marvel to co-found Image Comics and ran the WildStorm studio before selling it to DC in 1999 and joining the company himself.

His Batman: Hush with Jeph Loeb and his All Star Batman and Robin and Superman: For Tomorrow work made him DC's marquee artist, while his redesigns underpinned the New 52 relaunch, for which he served as co-publisher. He has since held DC's most senior creative posts, an unusual trajectory from superstar penciller to company leadership.

superman.name: Superman
superman.desc:
Created by Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster and first published in Action Comics #1 in 1938, Superman is the character from which the superhero genre descends: the secret identity, the costume, the powers used in public service, the newspaper-office supporting cast.

An immigrant survivor of a destroyed world raised in rural Kansas, he began as a crusading strongman against slum landlords and corrupt politicians and grew steadily more powerful and more cosmic through the 1950s and 1960s. He has been rebooted repeatedly — in 1986, in 2011 and again after Rebirth — and remains the property on which DC's identity rests.

batman.name: Batman
batman.desc:
Created by Bob Kane with Bill Finger and introduced in Detective Comics #27 in 1939, Batman is a wealthy orphan without superhuman powers who trains himself into a detective and vigilante after witnessing his parents' murder.

His tone has swung further than any comparable character's: pulp avenger in 1939, avuncular deputised policeman under the Comics Code, television camp in 1966, Bronze Age night creature under O'Neil and Adams, and grim myth after The Dark Knight Returns. He is DC's most commercially valuable character and the anchor of an unusually large family of related titles.

wonder_woman.name: Wonder Woman
wonder_woman.desc:
Created by William Moulton Marston with artist H. G. Peter and introduced in All Star Comics #8 in 1941, Wonder Woman was conceived as a deliberate corrective — a hero who would win through love and truth rather than force, and a model of female strength for child readers.

An Amazon princess from Themyscira with a lasso that compels truth, she is one of only three DC characters published continuously since the Golden Age. Her interpretation has shifted repeatedly, from Marston's idiosyncratic feminism through a powerless 1960s reinvention to George Pérez's 1987 relaunch grounding her firmly in Greek myth.

lois_lane.name: Lois Lane
lois_lane.desc:
Introduced alongside Superman in Action Comics #1, Lois Lane is a reporter at the Daily Planet whose pursuit of stories repeatedly outruns her own safety and whose scepticism about Clark Kent long structured the strip's central irony.

She was one of very few women to headline a mainstream superhero comic, in Superman's Girl Friend, Lois Lane, which ran from 1958 to 1974 and increasingly engaged with contemporary social questions. Later writers rebuilt her as an investigative journalist of the first rank rather than a romantic foil, and she married Clark Kent in 1996.

lex_luthor.name: Lex Luthor
lex_luthor.desc:
Superman's principal antagonist, introduced by Siegel and Shuster in 1940 as a red-haired mad scientist and settled into his familiar bald form shortly afterwards. For decades he was a criminal genius in a purple and green battlesuit driven by a personal grudge.

John Byrne's 1986 reboot recast him as a corporate billionaire whose power is legitimate and largely untouchable, making the conflict one of accountability rather than mad science. In that form he has been elected President of the United States within the fiction, and remains DC's most politically pointed villain.

supergirl.name: Supergirl
supergirl.desc:
Kara Zor-El, Superman's cousin, introduced by Otto Binder and Al Plastino in Action Comics #252 in 1959 as part of Mort Weisinger's expansion of the Superman mythos, and initially kept secret from the world as an emergency reserve.

Her death saving the multiverse in Crisis on Infinite Earths was one of the defining images of that series, and the post-Crisis rule that Superman be Krypton's only survivor kept her out of continuity for years. She returned in the 2000s and has since become a durable franchise in her own right in comics and on television.

dick_grayson.name: Dick Grayson / Robin
dick_grayson.desc:
The first Robin, introduced in Detective Comics #38 in 1940 as a circus acrobat orphaned by gangsters and taken in by Bruce Wayne. The character was created to give Batman someone to talk to and to give young readers a point of entry; sales rose sharply and kid sidekicks became a genre convention.

Grayson led the Teen Titans, broke with Batman and took the identity of Nightwing in 1984, and has periodically served as Batman himself. His progression from sidekick to independent hero is the template for legacy characters at DC.

joker.name: The Joker
joker.desc:
Introduced in Batman #1 in 1940, the Joker was conceived as a grinning murderer modelled in part on Conrad Veidt's face in The Man Who Laughs; Jerry Robinson, Bill Finger and Bob Kane have all been associated with his creation, and the credit is disputed.

He was softened into a harmless prankster under the Comics Code and returned to homicidal form in the 1970s under Denny O'Neil and Neal Adams. Later stories — The Killing Joke, A Death in the Family — made him the agent of permanent damage to Batman's world, and deliberately left his origin unfixed.

catwoman.name: Catwoman
catwoman.desc:
Selina Kyle, introduced as the Cat in Batman #1 in 1940 by Bill Finger and Bob Kane, a jewel thief written from the start as an antagonist Batman was unwilling to treat as a simple criminal.

The Comics Code's restrictions kept her out of print for more than a decade from the mid-1950s. She returned through the 1966 television series and was rebuilt in the 1980s, notably in Batman: Year One and in Ed Brubaker's run, into an anti-hero with her own long-running title and a durable moral ambiguity unusual for a Golden Age creation.

barbara_gordon.name: Barbara Gordon / Batgirl
barbara_gordon.desc:
Created by Gardner Fox and Carmine Infantino in 1967, partly at the request of the Batman television producers who wanted a new female lead, Barbara Gordon was a librarian and the police commissioner's daughter who became Batgirl.

Shot and paralysed by the Joker in The Killing Joke in 1988, she was reinvented by John Ostrander and Kim Yale as Oracle, the information broker at the centre of the DC universe's heroes and one of the few prominent disabled characters in superhero comics. She returned to walking and to the Batgirl identity in the 2011 relaunch, a decision that remains contested among readers.

jay_garrick.name: Jay Garrick / Flash
jay_garrick.desc:
The original Flash, created by Gardner Fox and Harry Lampert for Flash Comics #1 in 1940 — a college student who gains super-speed from inhaling hard water vapours and fights crime in a winged tin helmet borrowed from his father's war service.

A charter member of the Justice Society, Garrick was cancelled with the rest of the Golden Age heroes in the early 1950s. His reappearance in 1961 as an inhabitant of a parallel Earth in Flash of Two Worlds made him the first legacy figure in DC's continuity and gave the multiverse its founding logic.

barry_allen.name: Barry Allen / Flash
barry_allen.desc:
The Silver Age Flash, introduced in Showcase #4 in 1956: a methodical police scientist doused in chemicals struck by lightning, who takes his hero name from a comic book he read as a boy. His debut is conventionally treated as the beginning of the Silver Age.

Allen's sacrifice in Crisis on Infinite Earths in 1985 was among the first permanent deaths of a major superhero and stood for over two decades. Geoff Johns returned him in 2008, and his running through time to save his mother is the premise of Flashpoint, which triggered DC's 2011 relaunch.

wally_west.name: Wally West / Flash
wally_west.desc:
Introduced in 1959 as Kid Flash, Barry Allen's nephew by marriage, and a founding member of the Teen Titans. After Allen's death in Crisis on Infinite Earths he took the identity of the Flash — the first time at DC that a sidekick permanently replaced his mentor in a flagship role.

The promotion, and the long runs by William Messner-Loebs, Mark Waid and Geoff Johns that followed, made legacy succession a defining DC idea rather than a temporary stunt. His removal from continuity in the New 52 and restoration in Rebirth became a symbol of that argument.

alan_scott.name: Alan Scott / Green Lantern
alan_scott.desc:
The Golden Age Green Lantern, created by Martin Nodell with Bill Finger for All-American Comics #16 in 1940 — a railway engineer who survives a bridge collapse and forges a ring from a mystical green lantern, its power useless against wood.

Magical rather than science-fictional and unconnected to the later Green Lantern Corps, Scott was a charter member of the Justice Society. He returned as an Earth-Two character in the Silver Age and has since been written as one of DC's most prominent LGBT characters.

hal_jordan.name: Hal Jordan / Green Lantern
hal_jordan.desc:
The Silver Age Green Lantern, created by John Broome and Gil Kane in Showcase #22 in 1959: a test pilot chosen by a dying alien to join an interstellar police force whose ring can build anything its bearer imagines.

Jordan's reinvention converted a magical Golden Age hero into a space-opera franchise with the Guardians of the Universe, Oa and the Corps. Denny O'Neil sent him across America with Green Arrow to interrogate his own assumptions; he was later destroyed and rehabilitated across the 1990s and 2000s in one of DC's most contested character arcs.

john_stewart.name: John Stewart / Green Lantern
john_stewart.desc:
Created by Denny O'Neil and Neal Adams in 1971 as an architect recruited as a replacement Green Lantern, and among the first Black superheroes at DC. His introduction was written as a direct challenge to Hal Jordan's assumptions about who deserved authority.

After years as a substitute he became a lead Green Lantern in his own right. His prominence in Justice League and Justice League Unlimited, where Dwayne McDuffie was central to the writing, made him the version of the character most familiar to a mass audience.

aquaman.name: Aquaman
aquaman.desc:
Created by Mort Weisinger and Paul Norris in More Fun Comics #73 in 1941, one of the few Golden Age heroes to survive continuously into the Silver Age, when he was rewritten as Arthur Curry, heir to the throne of Atlantis.

A founding member of the Justice League, Aquaman spent decades as the butt of jokes about talking to fish, a reputation later writers attacked directly by emphasising the political burden of ruling an undersea kingdom in perpetual tension with the surface world. Peter David's 1990s run and the 2018 film substantially rehabilitated him.

green_arrow.name: Green Arrow
green_arrow.desc:
Created by Mort Weisinger and George Papp in More Fun Comics #73 in 1941, Oliver Queen began as a straightforward archery-themed hero with a sidekick, a signal-arrow gadget and an Arrowcar.

He was transformed in 1969 by Neal Adams's redesign and Denny O'Neil's writing into a bankrupt, bearded left-wing populist who argued with Hal Jordan across America about race and poverty — an unusually explicit political voice in mainstream comics. Mike Grell's Longbow Hunters later moved him into grounded urban crime drama.

martian_manhunter.name: Martian Manhunter
martian_manhunter.desc:
J'onn J'onzz, created by Joseph Samachson and Joe Certa in Detective Comics #225 in 1955, a Martian accidentally teleported to Earth who works as a human police detective — a science-fiction hero introduced before the Silver Age revivals proper, and sometimes cited as their forerunner.

A founding member of the Justice League and, in most versions, the last survivor of his species, he has been written increasingly as the team's emotional centre and its longest-serving member, the one who holds the League together between rosters.

darkseid.name: Darkseid
darkseid.desc:
Created by Jack Kirby for the Fourth World, appearing in Superman's Pal Jimmy Olsen in 1970 and fully in the following year, the ruler of Apokolips seeks the Anti-Life Equation — a formula that would extinguish free will everywhere.

Cold, static and unhurried where earlier villains were flamboyant, Darkseid became DC's default cosmic threat and the antagonist of Final Crisis, the Justice League's founding story in several continuities, and much of Superman's later mythology. He is the most widely used character to come out of Kirby's DC period.

swamp_thing.name: Swamp Thing
swamp_thing.desc:
Created by Len Wein and Bernie Wrightson in 1971, originally a scientist transformed by chemicals and fire into a shambling plant creature searching for his humanity — a horror hero made possible by the Comics Code's 1971 relaxation.

Alan Moore's 1984 revision reversed the premise entirely: the creature was never a man, but vegetable matter that had absorbed a dead man's memories and believed itself human. That single issue reset the character as an elemental force and made Swamp Thing the seedbed of what became Vertigo.

john_constantine.name: John Constantine
john_constantine.desc:
Introduced by Alan Moore, Stephen Bissette and John Totleben in Swamp Thing #37 in 1985, a working-class English occult confidence man who manipulates the powerful and survives by outliving the people around him. His appearance was modelled on the musician Sting.

His solo title Hellblazer launched in 1988, ran for three hundred issues and became Vertigo's longest-running series, ageing him in real time and using horror as a vehicle for commentary on Thatcher-era and post-Thatcher Britain.

harley_quinn.name: Harley Quinn
harley_quinn.desc:
Created by Paul Dini and Bruce Timm for Batman: The Animated Series in 1992 as a one-episode henchwoman for the Joker, and voiced by Arleen Sorkin. She proved so popular that she was written into the comics, first in Mad Love in 1994 and into mainstream continuity in 1999.

Harleen Quinzel, an Arkham psychiatrist seduced and abused by her patient, was gradually rewritten as an independent anti-hero who leaves the Joker. She is the most commercially successful character DC has created since the 1980s, and the clearest case of an adaptation feeding back into the source.

captain_marvel.name: Captain Marvel / Shazam
captain_marvel.desc:
Created by Bill Parker and C. C. Beck for Fawcett in 1940, Billy Batson is a homeless newsboy who becomes an adult superhero by speaking the wizard's name. Whimsical and warm where Superman was earnest, he outsold him through the 1940s.

National's infringement suit against Fawcett ended with Fawcett abandoning the character in 1953. DC licensed him in 1972 and bought him outright in 1991, but Marvel's trademark on the name meant DC could publish him only under the title Shazam!, which eventually became his name.

justice_society.name: Justice Society of America
justice_society.desc:
The first superhero team in comics, assembled by Gardner Fox in All Star Comics #3 in the winter of 1940 as a device to showcase characters from across the All-American and National lines in a single book, each taking a solo chapter of a shared case.

The Society disbanded in print in 1951 as the genre collapsed. Its members were later placed on the parallel Earth-Two, where they aged in real time, and the team became DC's vehicle for its own history — the generation that preceded and mentored everyone else.

justice_league.name: Justice League
justice_league.desc:
Introduced by Gardner Fox and Mike Sekowsky in The Brave and the Bold #28 in 1960, uniting Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, the Flash, Green Lantern, Aquaman and the Martian Manhunter as a modern successor to the Justice Society.

Its immediate success is widely credited with prompting the rival superhero team that became the Fantastic Four, and so with starting the Marvel age. The League has run through many formats — the satirical Justice League International, Grant Morrison's pantheon-scaled JLA — and remains DC's central shared-universe institution.

teen_titans.name: Teen Titans
teen_titans.desc:
A team of established sidekicks — Robin, Kid Flash, Aqualad and Wonder Girl — first gathered in the 1960s, allowing DC to write teenagers without disturbing the senior characters.

The 1980 relaunch as The New Teen Titans by Marv Wolfman and George Pérez, adding Raven, Cyborg and Starfire, became DC's best-selling title of the era and its answer to the X-Men. Its long-form serialised storytelling and its willingness to let sidekicks grow up produced Nightwing and set up much of Crisis on Infinite Earths.

suicide_squad.name: Suicide Squad
suicide_squad.desc:
Originally a 1959 adventure team, revived by John Ostrander in 1987 as Task Force X: imprisoned supervillains sent on deniable government missions in exchange for reduced sentences, with explosive implants ensuring compliance and a high casualty rate.

Run by Amanda Waller, the series worked as Cold War political thriller as much as superhero comic and made villains viable as leads. It is among the most heavily adapted DC properties of the last decade, in film, television and animation.

new_fun.name: New Fun / More Fun Comics
new_fun.desc:
New Fun #1, published by Malcolm Wheeler-Nicholson in early 1935, was a tabloid-sized anthology and one of the first American comic books made up entirely of original material rather than reprinted newspaper strips.

Renamed More Fun Comics, it became the company's longest thread back to its origins and later introduced the Spectre, Doctor Fate, Aquaman and Green Arrow. Its significance is less any single story than the proposition it proved: that a comic book could commission new work instead of recycling the funny pages.

action_comics.name: Action Comics
action_comics.desc:
Launched in 1938 as a general anthology, Action Comics #1 led with a thirteen-page Superman story bought for 130 dollars and carrying a cover of a man lifting a car over his head. Readers asked newsstands for the comic with Superman in it, and the industry changed within a year.

The title ran continuously for more than seven decades, was renumbered twice in modern relaunches and restored to its original numbering, and passed issue 1000 in 2018. Surviving copies of the first issue are the most valuable comic books in existence.

detective_comics_series.name: Detective Comics
detective_comics_series.desc:
Begun in March 1938 as a crime and mystery anthology, Detective Comics gave the company both its longest-running title and the two letters of its name. Its twenty-seventh issue, in May 1939, introduced Batman in a six-page story.

The title carried Batman thereafter and introduced Robin, the Joker's early appearances, Batgirl and the Martian Manhunter. Like Action Comics it has run essentially without interruption since the 1930s, and reached its thousandth issue in 2019.

all_star_comics.name: All Star Comics
all_star_comics.desc:
An All-American Publications anthology that in its third issue, in late 1940, gathered the company's heroes into the Justice Society of America — the first superhero team, and the origin of the shared-universe crossover as a commercial form.

Its eighth issue introduced Wonder Woman in a backup feature before she was given her own title. All Star ended in 1951, converted briefly into a western, and was revived in the 1970s, by which point the Justice Society had become the emblem of DC's own past.

showcase.name: Showcase
showcase.desc:
A try-out anthology launched in 1956 to test new concepts without committing to an ongoing series. Its fourth issue introduced Julius Schwartz's rebuilt Flash, and its success set the pattern for the entire Silver Age revival.

Showcase went on to introduce the Silver Age Green Lantern, the Challengers of the Unknown, Adam Strange, the Sea Devils and Metamorpho, among many others. No other title is as directly responsible for DC's post-war roster.

green_lantern_green_arrow.name: Green Lantern/Green Arrow
green_lantern_green_arrow.desc:
The run beginning with Green Lantern #76 in 1970, written by Denny O'Neil and drawn by Neal Adams, in which a Black man asks Hal Jordan why he has helped orange and purple skins but never his own people — and the hero has no answer.

The two heroes then travelled America arguing about racism, corporate exploitation, pollution and religious cults. The story in which Green Arrow's sidekick Speedy is found to be addicted to heroin was published with the Comics Code's newly relaxed rules. Critically celebrated and commercially unsuccessful, it defined what Bronze Age relevance meant.

new_gods.name: New Gods
new_gods.desc:
The centrepiece of Jack Kirby's Fourth World, launched in 1971: two worlds, the serene New Genesis and the industrial hell of Apokolips, locked in a war fought over the freedom of the mind rather than territory.

Kirby wrote, drew and edited an interconnected suite of titles introducing Darkseid, Orion, Mister Miracle, Big Barda and the Anti-Life Equation. Cancelled before its planned ending, the work was later recognised as one of the medium's great acts of world-building and has supplied villains and cosmology to DC ever since.

new_teen_titans.name: The New Teen Titans
new_teen_titans.desc:
Launched in 1980 by Marv Wolfman and George Pérez, the series took DC's grown-up sidekicks and added Raven, Cyborg and Starfire, running character-driven serialised stories with continuing consequences.

It became DC's best-selling comic of the early 1980s and its first genuine answer to the X-Men, producing the Judas Contract and Deathstroke, and giving Dick Grayson the room to become Nightwing. Its commercial success bought Wolfman and Pérez the standing to propose Crisis on Infinite Earths.

saga_of_the_swamp_thing.name: Saga of the Swamp Thing
saga_of_the_swamp_thing.desc:
Alan Moore took over a cancellation-bound title in 1984 and, in the issue titled The Anatomy Lesson, revealed that the creature had never been a transformed man at all — a reversal that turned a monster comic into a meditation on identity, ecology and the American South.

Drawn largely by Stephen Bissette, John Totleben and Rick Veitch, the run introduced John Constantine, dropped the Comics Code seal, and demonstrated that mature material could sell through the direct market. It is the immediate ancestor of Vertigo.

man_of_steel_1986.name: The Man of Steel
man_of_steel_1986.desc:
John Byrne's six-issue 1986 miniseries, commissioned to restart Superman from zero after Crisis on Infinite Earths removed nearly fifty years of accumulated continuity.

Byrne pared the character back: powers reduced, Krypton rendered cold and emotionally sterile, Superboy erased, the Kents alive to advise their adult son, Luthor rebuilt as a corporate predator, and Clark Kent treated as the real person rather than the disguise. The reboot was a commercial success and set the terms for the character until 2011.

dark_knight_returns.name: The Dark Knight Returns
dark_knight_returns.desc:
Frank Miller's four-part 1986 series showing a fifty-five-year-old Bruce Wayne coming out of retirement into a Gotham of gang violence, saturation television news and Cold War brinkmanship, ending in a confrontation with a state-sanctioned Superman.

Published in prestige format at a higher price, it proved that a comic could be sold as a book to adults, and its commercial success helped establish the graphic novel as a retail category. Its influence on the tone of subsequent superhero comics and films is difficult to overstate.

watchmen.name: Watchmen
watchmen.desc:
Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons's twelve-issue series, published from 1986, set in an America where costumed vigilantes are real, Nixon is still president and a single genuinely superhuman being has destabilised the Cold War.

Built on a rigid nine-panel grid with dense symmetry, embedded documents and a comic-within-the-comic, it treated the superhero as a political and psychological problem. It has never gone out of print, is routinely listed among the significant novels of the century, and its rights arrangement — under which the property never reverted to its creators — permanently soured Moore's relationship with DC.

batman_year_one.name: Batman: Year One
batman_year_one.desc:
Frank Miller and David Mazzucchelli's four-part 1987 story, published in Batman itself rather than as a separate miniseries, retelling Bruce Wayne's first year alongside Jim Gordon's arrival in a comprehensively corrupt Gotham police force.

Mazzucchelli's stripped-down art and Richmond Lewis's muted colour gave the story a crime-fiction register rather than a superheroic one. It became the accepted account of Batman's origin, displacing earlier versions, and supplied the framework for later screen adaptations.

sandman.name: The Sandman
sandman.desc:
Neil Gaiman's seventy-five-issue series, begun in 1989, about Dream of the Endless — one of seven personifications older than gods — who is imprisoned for seventy years and must rebuild his kingdom, and himself, afterwards.

Drawing on myth, folklore, history and literature, and drawn by a rotating cast of artists including Sam Kieth, Kelley Jones, Marc Hempel and P. Craig Russell under Dave McKean's covers, it reached readers who had never bought a comic before. Gaiman ended it deliberately in 1996 rather than let it continue without him.

all_star_superman.name: All-Star Superman
all_star_superman.desc:
Grant Morrison and Frank Quitely's twelve-issue series, published from 2005 outside regular continuity, in which Superman is fatally overexposed to solar radiation and sets about completing twelve final labours.

Affectionate towards the strangest material of the Weisinger era while entirely modern in construction, it argued that the character's optimism is his point rather than his limitation. It is widely regarded as the best modern Superman story and directly informed later screen interpretations.

crisis_on_infinite_earths.name: Crisis on Infinite Earths
crisis_on_infinite_earths.desc:
The twelve-issue series by Marv Wolfman and George Pérez, published across 1985 and 1986 for DC's fiftieth anniversary, in which an antimatter wave destroys the multiverse and the survivors emerge into a single merged universe with a single history.

It was conceived as a solution to decades of accumulated parallel Earths that editorial believed were deterring new readers. Supergirl and Barry Allen died; every title was affected. It established the line-wide crossover as a commercial fixture and set a pattern of periodic continuity resets that DC has followed ever since.

death_of_superman.name: The Death of Superman
death_of_superman.desc:
The 1992 storyline in which Superman is beaten to death by the monster Doomsday, followed by Funeral for a Friend, Reign of the Supermen and his eventual return roughly a year later.

Covered as news by mainstream media worldwide, it produced the biggest single sales spike in modern comics and drew enormous numbers of speculative buyers who never returned. The episode is a central exhibit in accounts of the 1990s speculator bubble and of the industry's near-collapse when that bubble burst.

flashpoint.name: Flashpoint
flashpoint.desc:
Geoff Johns and Andy Kubert's 2011 crossover, in which Barry Allen wakes into a world where his mother is alive, Thomas Wayne is Batman, and Atlantis and Themyscira are at war — the consequence of his own journey back through time to prevent her murder.

Repairing the damage required Barry to let his mother die again, and the reconstituted timeline was not the one he left. Flashpoint served as the narrative mechanism for the New 52, folding the WildStorm and Vertigo characters into a single continuity.

new_52.name: The New 52
new_52.desc:
DC's September 2011 relaunch, in which the entire line was cancelled and restarted with fifty-two new first issues under co-publishers Dan DiDio and Jim Lee, with continuity reset to a universe five years old and every title released digitally the same day as in print.

The move produced a substantial short-term sales increase and drew back lapsed readers, but the compressed history discarded marriages, legacies and characters that long-time readers valued — most contentiously Wally West and the Justice Society — and much of it was reversed within five years.

dc_rebirth.name: DC Rebirth
dc_rebirth.desc:
The 2016 relaunch initiated by Geoff Johns in DC Universe: Rebirth #1, framed explicitly as a correction to the New 52: the missing years, relationships and legacies had been stolen from the universe by an outside force, and Wally West's return was the story's emotional centre.

Rebirth restored twice-monthly publication at a lower price, brought back the pre-Flashpoint Superman and his family, and reintroduced the Justice Society. It also set up Doomsday Clock, which folded the Watchmen characters into DC continuity.

batman_1966.name: Batman (1966 television series)
batman_1966.desc:
The ABC series starring Adam West and Burt Ward, broadcast twice weekly from 1966, which played Batman as deadpan camp in saturated colour with onomatopoeic fight captions and a rotating cast of guest villains.

It was an immediate international phenomenon and briefly lifted comics sales enormously, and it prompted DC to add Batgirl to the comics and to the show. When the fashion passed, the series left the character indelibly associated with silliness — a reputation Denny O'Neil and later Frank Miller spent decades undoing.

superman_1978.name: Superman (1978 film)
superman_1978.desc:
Richard Donner's film, starring Christopher Reeve with Marlon Brando and Gene Hackman, was made on a scale no comic book adaptation had previously attempted and marketed on the promise that audiences would believe a man could fly.

Its commercial and critical success established the superhero film as a serious studio proposition and demonstrated to Warner the value of the characters it had bought in 1967. Reeve's performance, which took the character's sincerity seriously, remained the reference point for decades.

batman_1989.name: Batman (1989 film)
batman_1989.desc:
Tim Burton's film, with Michael Keaton as Batman and Jack Nicholson as the Joker, drew on the darker comics of the preceding years and on Anton Furst's gothic Gotham to erase the public memory of the 1966 series.

It was one of the highest-grossing films of its year and its merchandising campaign was unprecedented, proving that DC's characters were valuable to Warner far beyond publishing. Its success led directly to Batman: The Animated Series and to three sequels of declining quality.

batman_animated_series.name: Batman: The Animated Series
batman_animated_series.desc:
The 1992 series developed by Bruce Timm and Eric Radomski, animated on black paper to give Gotham a permanently nocturnal art-deco look, with a symphonic score and voice performances by Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill that became definitive.

It treated its villains as tragedies rather than gimmicks, won critical respect unusual for children's television, and created Harley Quinn. Its style extended into Superman, Batman Beyond and Justice League Unlimited, forming a coherent animated universe that shaped a generation's sense of the characters.

dark_knight_film.name: The Dark Knight
dark_knight_film.desc:
Christopher Nolan's 2008 film, the second of his trilogy, treating Gotham as a plausible modern city and the Joker, played by Heath Ledger, as an agent of pure disorder testing whether institutions and individuals hold under pressure.

It earned Ledger a posthumous Academy Award, passed a billion dollars at the box office, and made the case that superhero films could be treated as serious cinema. Its influence pushed Warner and its competitors towards darker, more realistic adaptations for the following decade.

marvel_comics.name: Marvel Comics
marvel_comics.desc:
The rival publisher, founded as Timely Comics in 1939 and branding its covers Marvel from 1963. Its 1961 relaunch under Stan Lee and Jack Kirby was commissioned after DC's Justice League demonstrated that superhero teams could sell again, and it answered DC's clean, rationalised house style with continuity, argument and heroes who had money troubles.

Marvel overtook DC in market share in the early 1970s and held the lead for most of the following two decades, a reversal that drove much of DC's response: the recruitment of Kirby in 1970, the editorial reforms of the Kahn era, and the eventual turn towards prestige and creator-driven publishing. Staff have moved between the two companies continuously.

jimmy_olsen.name: Superman's Pal, Jimmy Olsen
jimmy_olsen.desc:
A long-running Superman spin-off that became, unexpectedly, the entry point for Jack Kirby's DC career. Offered his choice of assignment in 1970, Kirby asked for the title precisely because it was selling badly and had no regular creative team, so that taking it would cost nobody their job.

He took over with issue 133 and used it to introduce the Newsboy Legion's successors, the DNA Project and, in issue 134, the first glimpse of Darkseid. DC had his Superman faces redrawn by staff artists to preserve the house look — an editorial decision Kirby resented and which is visible on the page.

forever_people.name: The Forever People
forever_people.desc:
One of the three titles Kirby launched in 1971 to carry the Fourth World, following a group of young New Genesis characters who arrive on Earth searching for a missing friend and who summon a single warrior, the Infinity Man, by joining hands.

Its first issue contains Darkseid's first full appearance, and its counterculture register — communal, itinerant, suspicious of authority — is the most explicitly of-its-moment thing Kirby produced at DC. It was cancelled after eleven issues in 1972, before its story could be completed.

mister_miracle_title.name: Mister Miracle
mister_miracle_title.desc:
The Fourth World title that outlived the rest, running to eighteen issues before its 1974 cancellation and revived repeatedly since. It follows an escape artist raised in Apokolips's orphanage who has made a career out of the one skill that upbringing taught him.

Kirby wrote and drew it as the most personal of the four books: the escape is the point, and every trap is a version of the same one. It introduced Big Barda and Granny Goodness, and Tom King and Mitch Gerads's 2017 revival — which read the escapes as a study of trauma and depression — is among the most acclaimed DC comics of the last decade.

kamandi.name: Kamandi, the Last Boy on Earth
kamandi.desc:
Kirby's post-apocalyptic series, begun in 1972, following a boy raised in a bunker into a ruined North America governed by intelligent animal societies — tiger warlords, dog scientists, ape gangs — with humanity reduced to livestock.

It was his best-selling DC title of the period, outlasting the Fourth World books that had been the point of hiring him, and ran to fifty-nine issues with Kirby writing and drawing the first forty. Its treatment of ruin as an adventure playground rather than a tragedy has been widely imitated since.

scott_free.name: Scott Free / Mister Miracle
scott_free.desc:
The son of Highfather of New Genesis, handed to Darkseid as a child under a peace treaty that exchanged the two rulers' sons, and raised in Granny Goodness's orphanage on Apokolips.

He escapes to Earth, apprentices himself to a stage escapologist and takes his name, turning an upbringing designed to break him into a career performing impossible escapes. Kirby made the metaphor explicit rather than incidental, and later writers — Grant Morrison in Seven Soldiers, Tom King in 2017 — have built their runs on it. He served for years in the Justice League's International era.

big_barda.name: Big Barda
big_barda.desc:
Commander of Darkseid's Female Furies, trained from childhood as a soldier of Apokolips, who defects for Scott Free and follows him to Earth.

Kirby wrote her as physically the stronger of the pair and entirely unembarrassed by it, and their marriage as a settled partnership rather than a romance in progress — an unusual arrangement for a superhero comic of 1971, and the reason the two characters have remained inseparable in every later treatment.

orion.name: Orion
orion.desc:
Darkseid's son, given to Highfather in the exchange that sent Scott Free to Apokolips, and raised on New Genesis by the enemy of his father.

Orion is the Fourth World's central argument in one figure: a being whose inherited rage is visible whenever his Astro-Force harness fails, permanently uncertain whether he is his upbringing or his blood. Kirby wrote the war between the worlds as ending in a prophesied confrontation between father and son, which the cancellation of the titles left unpublished for years.

final_crisis.name: Final Crisis
final_crisis.desc:
Grant Morrison's 2008 crossover, drawn principally by J. G. Jones and Doug Mahnke, built on the premise that the war Kirby described had already been lost: Darkseid has fallen through reality onto Earth, and the Anti-Life Equation is loose and spreading through the population as a formula that ends free will.

Structured in fragments and elliptical jumps rather than conventional crossover beats, it divided readers sharply. It also brought the Fourth World back to the centre of DC's cosmology, and removed Batman from continuity for a year via Darkseid's Omega Sanction.

links.details: Wheeler-Nicholson set up National Allied Publications in 1934 on almost no capital, betting that readers would buy a magazine of original comics rather than newspaper reprints. The bet was correct; his finances were not, and he never saw the profits.

Unable to fund a third title alone, Wheeler-Nicholson formed Detective Comics, Inc. in 1937 as a partnership with his printer and distributor. It was the arrangement that gave DC both its most valuable title and its name — and cost him his company.
Donenfeld put up the money and the presses for the new venture, taking an equity position in the partnership. Within a year he had used Wheeler-Nicholson's unpaid debts to take the whole business.
Liebowitz held the books and the other half of Donenfeld's interest, and it was he who managed the bankruptcy proceedings that removed Wheeler-Nicholson from the company he had started.

When National Allied went into bankruptcy in 1938, Donenfeld and Liebowitz bought its assets — including an unpublished Superman story already scheduled for Action Comics #1 — and merged the line into their own.

The founder was forced out of his own firm months before Superman made it rich. Wheeler-Nicholson received a modest settlement and no share of what followed; the episode set an early pattern for how the company handled the people who brought it its properties.

The partnership of the flamboyant pulp publisher and the meticulous accountant ran the company for three decades. Donenfeld was the name and the personality; Liebowitz made the decisions that mattered and outlasted him.

New Fun #1, dated February 1935, was National Allied's first release and one of the first American comic books composed entirely of new material. It lost money, but it established that comics could be commissioned rather than recycled.

Detective Comics #1 appeared in March 1938 as a themed crime anthology — an unusual idea at a time when comic books were general grab-bags. Its title supplied the two initials the publisher has used ever since.

National Allied is the root of the corporate line that runs through Detective Comics, Inc. and National Periodical Publications to the modern DC Comics — an unbroken commercial descent from a bankrupt 1930s pulp operation.

The partnership's name outlived the partnership. Consolidated with National Allied and later renamed National Comics Publications, the firm kept using DC as a cover logo for four decades before adopting it formally in 1977.

Liebowitz shaped the company more than any other executive of its first thirty years: he financed All-American, unified the two lines in 1946, kept the publisher on the right side of the Comics Code, and sold the whole business to Kinney National in 1967.

Liebowitz put up the backing for Gaines's new company in 1939 while keeping it formally separate from National — an arrangement that spread the financial risk and left him with leverage over both halves of the business.

Gaines ran All-American as a distinct editorial operation with its own offices and its own editor, and produced a strikingly large share of the Golden Age canon: the Flash, Green Lantern, the Justice Society and Wonder Woman all came from his line.

Gaines sold his interest in 1946 and All-American was absorbed into National Comics Publications, formally merging the two halves of what readers had always treated as one publisher because they shared a cover logo.

With the proceeds of the All-American sale Gaines started a small educational comics line, and after his death in a 1947 boating accident his son William turned it into EC — the horror and satire publisher that the Comics Code was largely designed to destroy.
Gaines is generally credited with passing the rejected Superman samples on to Vin Sullivan at National, the referral that put the strip into Action Comics #1 after five years of rejections.

By Mayer's own later account, he retrieved the Superman submission from the reject pile as Gaines's young assistant and argued repeatedly that it should be published — an editorial judgement that decided the shape of the industry.

Mayer edited All-American's whole line in his twenties, overseeing Flash Comics, All-American Comics and All Star Comics, and hiring and shielding the creators who built the company's Golden Age roster.

All Star Comics was All-American's showcase anthology, and the book in which Mayer and Gardner Fox gathered the line's heroes into a single team — the format innovation that made the shared universe a commercial proposition.

National sued Fawcett for infringing Superman with Captain Marvel, and the litigation ran through the 1940s and into the early 1950s. With superhero sales collapsing anyway, Fawcett settled and stopped publishing the character in 1953.

DC licensed the Fawcett superheroes in 1972 and bought them outright in 1991 — acquiring the character it had spent a decade suing out of print, though Marvel's trademark on the name meant it could only be sold as Shazam!

Whiz Comics #2 introduced Captain Marvel in 1940, and by mid-decade Captain Marvel Adventures was outselling Superman — the commercial fact that made National's infringement suit worth pursuing so relentlessly.
DC bought Charlton's superhero characters in 1983 as the smaller publisher left the business, picking up the Question, Blue Beetle, Captain Atom, Peacemaker and Nightshade for a modest sum.

Kinney National Company bought National Periodical Publications in 1967 and, after absorbing Warner Bros.-Seven Arts, renamed itself Warner Communications in 1972. DC has been a subsidiary of a large media conglomerate ever since, through Time Warner, WarnerMedia and Warner Bros. Discovery.
Liebowitz negotiated the 1967 sale and took a seat on the acquiring company's board, converting his publishing business into a corporate position and setting DC's future as one asset among many.

Vertigo was launched in 1993 as DC's mature-readers imprint, publishing without the Comics Code seal and on terms closer to creator ownership. It gave the company literary standing and a second audience that the superhero line could not reach.

Berger proposed gathering the adult titles she was already editing under a single imprint and ran it as executive editor for twenty years, defining its house style: literate, unheroic, and dominated by British writers she had personally recruited.

Kahn's insistence that DC compete on prestige rather than imitate Marvel, and her willingness to publish outside the Comics Code, created the conditions in which an imprint like Vertigo could be proposed at all.
